landscapes-physical-processes: Why are most of Britain's mountains in the north and west, and its flattest land in the south and east?
Walkers, sheep farmers, quarries and boats all want the same fells. Who gets to use the Lake District?
A silt grain is one-hundredth the width of a coarse sand grain, yet water must flow about three times as fast to pick it up. Why?
Niagara Falls has moved about 7 miles (11 km) upstream in about 12,000 years. How does a waterfall move backwards?
Between 1951 and 2004 the cliffs at Aldbrough, on England's Holderness coast, retreated about 2 m a year. Why do they disappear so fast?
Spurn Point is over three miles long and in places only 50 m wide. How did a finger of sand form across the mouth of the Humber?
Why do some UK coastlines and rivers change many times faster than others?
At any moment, rivers hold only about 0.006% of Earth's fresh water. So how does a river keep flowing through weeks without rain?

On 23 December 2013, 43–45 mm of rain fell on two river basins in southern England. Within a day, one river surged to one of its highest flows since records began; the other barely rose, and peaked only in mid-February after weeks more rain. Why did the same storm have such different effects?
A study found that urbanisation made Hurricane Harvey-scale flooding in Houston's basins about 21 times as likely in 2017. How can a city make a flood worse?
For weeks in 2014, some Somerset villages could only be reached by boat. Why did the floods last so long?
In 1995, more than 250,000 people in the Netherlands had to leave their homes as the rivers rose. The Dutch response was not simply higher dikes. What did they do?
rural-urban-links: London is more than 600 times as crowded as the Highlands. Why do people cluster where they do?
In one year, about 339,000 people moved into England's mostly rural council areas. What does that do to villages?
Why are some UK villages growing fast while others are losing people?
In one English district a third of people are 65 or over; in another, one in eighteen. What makes a place old?
London builds most of its new homes on old, used land. Why not just build on the fields around it?
Over a quarter of retail spending in Great Britain now happens online. So what is the high street for?
In 1979 Shenzhen was what its government calls "a small backward border town". By 2024 it had 17.98 million residents. Where did they all come from?
Mumbai keeps drawing people in from across India. Who really gains from its growth?
London produces more per person than any other UK region. So why can so many Londoners not afford a home?
London and Mumbai are on different continents. What ties each of them so tightly to the rest of the world?
coastal-hazards-management: What can push the sea far enough inland to flood a whole coastline?
By 2014 the Environment Agency had built new banks inland at Medmerry, West Sussex, and let the sea flood the land between. Why give land to the sea?
Why does England defend some stretches of coast and let the sea take others?
About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level. Tuvalu's land averages about 2 m above it. Which is more vulnerable, and why?
tectonic-landscapes-and-hazards: The Atlantic is about 2.5 cm wider every year. What moves the plates?
In 1985 a volcano 45 km away killed about 23,000 people in Armero, two hours after it erupted. How?
In one Aceh village, the 2004 tsunami killed four females for every male. Why would a wave "choose"?
Nepal 2015 and Kaikōura 2016 were both magnitude 7.8. One killed more than 8,790 people; the other killed 2. Why?
On Fuego, in 2018, a golf resort evacuated safely. A village two kilometres further on was buried. Why?
About 800 million people live near active volcanoes. Why don't they move away?
weather-climate-and-ecosystems: How do scientists know what Earth's climate was like 800,000 years ago, long before thermometers?
Most of Earth's carbon is locked away in rock. So why does burning a little of it matter so much?
In 1991 one volcano in the Philippines cooled the whole planet. How?
Why are the world's rainforests and hottest deserts found in bands either side of the equator?
Hurricane Ian hit Florida with 130-knot winds in 2022. Why was water, not wind, its deadliest hazard?
A hurricane hit Cuba, then Florida. The USA is far richer than Cuba, so why did far more people die in Florida?
In June 2021 a Canadian village reached 49.6 °C, a national record. Could that have happened without climate change?
The wettest Scottish mountains get about eight times the rain of the driest parts of eastern England. Why?
Why is British weather so changeable, yet sometimes settled for weeks on end?
development-and-resource-issues: Guyana's income per person is more than three and a half times Sri Lanka's. Why do they have exactly the same HDI?
India now has more people than any other country. Why is it still only a lower-middle-income country?
In 1994 Rwanda's economy shrank by half. What has shaped its development since?
Why does a baby born in Norway expect to live about 25 years longer than one born in Somalia?
In 2020 Indonesia stopped exporting nickel ore. By 2025 it mined most of the world's nickel. Who gains when a country closes a door?

Apple employs about 166,000 people. Toyota and its affiliates run more than 50 manufacturing operations in 27 countries and regions outside Japan. Why do these two giants make their products in such different ways?
Tourism makes up about a fifth of the Maldives' economy. Yet in 2022 most people working in its resorts were not Maldivian. Who really gains from a resort?
In 2017 Rwanda doubled the price of a permit to see mountain gorillas, to US$1,500. Can making tourism more expensive make it more sustainable?
Thailand welcomed almost 40 million foreign tourists in one year. Who in Thailand actually gained?
In 2022 Sri Lanka defaulted on its foreign debt and turned to the IMF. Who sets the terms of rescue loans, and is there an alternative?
In 2006 a bank for poor villagers won the Nobel Peace Prize. Do small loans and fairer prices really lift people out of poverty?
social-development-issues: Is the gap in how long people live between rich and poor countries closing, or getting wider?
At today's rate, Niger's population would double in about 21 years. Japan's is shrinking. Why?
Why do millions of children go to work instead of school, and what gets them back into class?
Within a year of August 2017, nearly 725,000 people had fled from Myanmar into Bangladesh. Why do so many people flee at once, and what happens where they arrive?
Why do so many babies in sub-Saharan Africa die before their first birthday, when most causes are preventable?
Malaria killed an estimated 610,000 people in 2024. Why does it kill mostly in one continent, and mostly young children?
New HIV infections have fallen 65% since their peak in 1994. Was that prevention or treatment, and why are some groups still left behind?
environmental-challenges: If everyone lived like the average person in Qatar, humanity would use up a whole year's worth of nature by 4 February. If everyone lived like the average person in India, the year's supply would not run out before the year ended. What is being measured?
China imported about ten times as many soybeans in 2023 as in 2000. In 2025, nearly three in four came from Brazil. Why does what people eat in China matter to land in Brazil?
Transporting the world's fruit and vegetables releases almost twice as much greenhouse gas as growing them. So is "buy local" the answer?
In 2016, China reported importing about 8.8 million tonnes of plastic waste. In 2018, it imported about 51,000 tonnes. What happened, and where did the waste go?
England has had three droughts in five years, yet UK records show part of the year getting wetter. How can both be true?
Rotterdam to Yokohama is about 11,200 nautical miles via Suez, but about 6,500 over the top of the world. Will melting ice make the Arctic a new shipping highway?
The least developed countries emitted less than 0.4% of all historical fossil CO₂, yet face some of the worst impacts. Who should cut emissions, and who should pay?
Since 1970 the world has lost about 22% of its wetlands. Can a plan for a whole river basin bring a wetland back?
Thailand closed one of its most famous beaches to visitors for about three and a half years. Why would a country shut a beach that tourists love?
development-and-resource-issues-part-2: Producing 1 kg of beef takes about 15,400 litres of water, on a world average. Is beef draining the world's rivers?

The Lower Mekong's fisheries land an estimated 2.3 million tonnes of fish a year, worth about US$11 billion. Its hydropower capacity could more than double. Can one river be both a great fishery and a giant power station?
About 85% of the Nile's water starts in Ethiopia, yet a 1959 agreement shared it between Egypt and Sudan. Who decides how it is used now, and what would make a deal work?
Farms on the US High Plains pump water from underground. What happens when they take more than rain puts back?
Can one label tell you how rich a country is, when its own regions are worlds apart?
A baby boy in Hart, Hampshire can expect to live ten years longer than one in Blackpool. Why?
Can a new factory or a new railway help a poorer region of the UK catch up?
weather-climate-and-ecosystems-part-2: Rainforest at the equator, desert a little further north. Why do the world's big ecosystems come in bands?
Rainforest soils are surprisingly poor. So how do they grow such huge, rich forests?
Coral reefs grow in clear seas with few nutrients, yet they teem with life. How?
What happens to a whole pond when just one thing in it changes?
Forests, reefs and rivers feed, shelter and protect us for free. So why do we keep cutting them down?
A dam across the Severn could turn its enormous tides into electricity. Why has it never been built?
The world's biggest rainforest is still being cleared. Who is doing it, and why does it matter beyond Brazil?
How can a farm far inland, or a fishing boat, push coral species towards extinction?
Some villagers in Guatemala make a living by cutting down rainforest trees. Can logging help save a forest?
A community on Kenya's coast earns money by not cutting down its mangroves. Who pays, and why?
